text: Last lesson of the chapter. The Analytics pane adds real analytical power directly on top of a chart you've already built — no separate visual type required, no rebuilding anything from scratch.

The most common addition by far is a reference line. Select a line type, select Add, name it, and pick the measure it's based on — here, an average line labeled Average sales, showing exactly how each data point compares to the mean. Power BI supports several other line types too: min, max, median, percentile, and constant lines fixed to a specific axis value — and you can add more than one of the same type together, each with its own name and color.

With genuine time-series data on a line chart, Forecast projects future values forward based on the historical trend already in your model. The shaded band around that projection is the confidence interval — how certain the prediction actually is, naturally widening the further out it tries to look. Forecasting and anomaly detection both share one requirement: a line chart with real dates on the axis, since neither has anything to project without one.

And beyond the Analytics pane itself, a handful of AI-powered visuals are worth recognizing even without a full deep dive here. Decomposition tree lets viewers drill across multiple dimensions in whatever order they choose, with AI suggesting what to explore next. Key influencers surfaces which factors most affect a selected result. Smart narrative automatically writes plain-language text calling out the trends and takeaways sitting behind a visual.
Ten lessons, and one full report of the right visuals, properly filtered, properly connected, and genuinely analyzed. Next up: Chapter Eight, Dashboard Design and Storytelling.
